What Is THCA? How It Differs From THC and Why It Matters

THCA is the raw form of THC that cannabis plants make. Learn how heat converts it, how to read THCA and total THC on a label, and what Michigan law says about THCA flower.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20269 min read

09min readResources
In this article
  1. What THCA is and where it's found
  2. How THCA interacts with the body (what's known)
  3. Early research on THCA, and what's unproven
  4. Decarboxylation: how heat turns THCA into THC
  5. THC vs. THCA side by side
  6. How THCA differs from THCV
  7. Why labels show THCA and how to work out total THC
  8. THCA flower, hemp shops and the law
  9. Choosing products by THCA and total THC
  10. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • THCA is the acid form of THC that the plant makes; the heat of smoking, vaping or baking converts it into THC.
  • On its own, THCA shows little activity at the receptors THC acts on and doesn't produce a high.
  • Total THC = THC + (THCA × 0.877), the formula labs use to estimate potency after heating.
  • As of October 2026, Michigan law counts THCA as THC, so flower above 0.3% THC, counting THCA, is marijuana that only licensed businesses may sell.
  • Most of the research on raw THCA comes from lab and animal studies; human evidence is thin.

THC vs. THCA is really a before-and-after story. THCA is the form the cannabis plant actually makes, and THC is what most of it becomes when heated. That's why raw flower can carry a high THCA number yet produce its familiar effects only once it's smoked, vaped or cooked. Here's what THCA is, what research shows about it, how to read it on a label and what Michigan law says about it.

What THCA is and where it's found

THCA, short for tetrahydrocannabinolic acid, is the acidic precursor of THC. The plant builds it in the resin glands, or trichomes, that frost its flowers. In the plant, THCA can account for up to 90% of the total THC.

THCA starts from a parent compound called CBGA, which the plant can also turn into CBDA, the acid form of CBD. Each strain's genetics steer more of that parent compound one way or the other. That's why most dispensary flower is rich in THCA, while hemp grown for CBD leans toward CBDA.

You'll find THCA in raw and fresh-frozen flower, in many extracts and, most visibly, in THCA diamonds, crystals made mostly of THCA. It slowly turns into THC on its own during storage, but the big change comes with heat.

How THCA interacts with the body (what's known)

THC causes its high mainly by acting on the CB1 receptor in the brain. THCA doesn't fit that receptor well. In a 2017 laboratory study, THCA showed little affinity or activity at either main cannabinoid receptor, CB1 or CB2, while THC bound to CB1 about 62 times more strongly.

A review of THCA research reaches the same practical conclusion: unlike THC, THCA doesn't produce psychoactive effects in humans. One complication runs through the science, though. THCA converts to THC so easily that the 2017 study's authors called some THC contamination of samples nearly unavoidable, which can muddy results.

Early research on THCA, and what's unproven

Scientists are interested in THCA because lab studies suggest it interacts with a number of molecular targets beyond the cannabinoid receptors. Most of that work has been done in cell cultures and animals. Human studies are scarce, and reviewers say more experiments are needed before drawing conclusions.

Until that research exists, claims about raw THCA, from juiced leaves to THCA tinctures, remain unproven. If you're considering THCA for a health reason, talk with your clinician first, and remember that heated THCA is simply THC.

Raw THCA turns up in a few forms: fresh leaves or flower blended into juice, tinctures made without heat, and isolated THCA crystals. Each usually carries some THC, and heat during processing or storage can convert more of it over time. If you want to avoid intoxication, check the label's THC figure, not just the THCA.

Decarboxylation: how heat turns THCA into THC

Decarboxylation is the chemical step that turns THCA into THC. Heat knocks a small carboxyl group off each THCA molecule, releasing it as carbon dioxide, and what's left is THC. It happens rapidly when you smoke or vape flower, and over the course of a bake in the oven.

ProcessWhat happens to THCA
Smoking or vapingConverts rapidly as the flower heats
Baking or decarbing in an ovenConverts during the bake
StorageConverts slowly over time
Raw, unheated flowerStays mostly THCA

Heat and time have to be balanced. Too little leaves THCA unconverted, while too much starts breaking THC down, partly into CBN, a milder cannabinoid. That's why edible recipes call for heating flower at a low, steady oven temperature before you infuse it, a step covered in our guide to decarboxylation.

THC vs. THCA side by side

THCATHC (delta-9)
What it isThe acid form the plant makesThe active form, mostly created by heat
Where you'll find itRaw and fresh-frozen flower, diamondsSmoked or vaped flower, edibles, distillate
Causes a high?No, not unless heated into THCYes
Fit at the CB1 receptorLittle affinity in lab testsBinds strongly: about 62 times THCA's affinity in one study
On a labelOften listed separatelyOften a small number on raw flower
Under Michigan lawCounts toward THCCounts toward THC

THC itself comes in more than one form. For delta-8 and the rest of the family, see our guide to different types of THC.

How THCA differs from THCV

The names are one letter apart, but THCV isn't a form of THCA. THCV, or tetrahydrocannabivarin, is a separate cannabinoid with a slightly different structure, usually found in small amounts. It has its own acid form, THCVA, which heat converts the same way.

THCATHCV
Relationship to THCTHC's acid precursorA related but separate cannabinoid
Typical amountOften the main cannabinoid in raw flowerUsually a minor component
EffectsNo high unless heated into THCStill being studied; findings are mixed

Research on THCV is early, and it usually appears in small amounts, so check the lab results if it matters to you. Our explainer on THCV and its effects covers what's known so far.

Why labels show THCA and how to work out total THC

Lab reports for flower often list THCA and delta-9 THC separately, because most of the THC in unheated flower is still THCA. To estimate how much THC you'll get once it's heated, labs use a total THC calculation:

Total THC = THC + (THCA × 0.877)

The 0.877 accounts for the weight THCA loses when it sheds its carboxyl group. For example, flower that tests at 24% THCA and 1% THC works out to 1 + (24 × 0.877), or about 22% total THC. A gram of diamonds at 95% THCA holds about 830 mg of potential THC (950 mg × 0.877). Total THC is the number to compare between products.

What you'll see depends on the product:

ProductTypical label patternWhat to compare
Flower and pre-rollsHigh THCA, low delta-9 THCTotal THC
Diamonds and other THCA-rich extractsVery high THCATotal THC, and keep portions tiny
Vape carts made with distillateMostly THC alreadyTHC percentage
Edibles and drinksTHC in milligrams, already heatedmg per serving

Our guide to reading a cannabis label shows where these figures appear on a package.

THCA flower, hemp shops and the law

"THCA flower" is often sold outside licensed dispensaries as hemp, on the theory that its delta-9 THC is low even though its THCA is high. Once you smoke it, that THCA becomes THC, so it acts like any other cannabis flower.

In Michigan, as of October 2026, the law counts THCA as THC. Cannabis testing above 0.3% THC, THCA included, is marijuana, and only licensed marijuana businesses may sell it. At 0.3% or less, it's industrial hemp, which falls under separate rules. So is THCA flower legal in Michigan? Flower above that line can be sold only by licensed cannabis businesses, to adults 21 and older or registered medical patients.

At the federal level, a law passed in November 2025 redefines hemp to cap total THC, THCA included, at 0.3%. It also excludes finished hemp products with more than 0.4 mg of total THC per container. As of October 2026, the new definition is set to apply from November 12, 2026 to products with cannabinoids the plant can't make naturally, and to everything else from December 11, 2026. Those dates can still change.

Our explainer on hemp vs. marijuana covers the difference in detail, and our Michigan cannabis laws guide covers possession and purchase limits.

Choosing products by THCA and total THC

  • Compare total THC, not just THC. A flower label showing 1% THC and 25% THCA describes a strong product once heated.
  • Read total THC as an upper estimate. The formula assumes every bit of THCA converts, and real-world smoking and vaping lose some along the way.
  • Raw products work differently. Unheated THCA products won't produce the usual high, but they often contain some THC, so read the label.
  • Diamonds are potent. THCA crystals become highly concentrated THC when dabbed, so a tiny amount goes a long way.
  • Buy licensed. Licensed Michigan products are lab tested, and the label shows their THC content.

Your goal decides what to look for:

  • You want the familiar effects of cannabis. Any heated product delivers THC. Compare total THC on flower and THC milligrams on edibles, and start low.
  • You're curious about raw THCA. Know that human research is thin, check the THC on the label, and talk with your clinician if you have a health reason in mind.
  • You're sensitive to THC. Choose products with lower total THC and smaller servings, and give each one time before taking more.

At High Society, our budtenders can answer questions about the THCA and total THC numbers on a label and help you compare flower, vapes and concentrates. Order ahead for in-store or curbside pickup, and bring a valid photo ID: shopping is for adults 21 and older, or 18 and older with a valid medical marijuana card.

Frequently asked questions

Does THCA get you high?

Not on its own. THCA shows little activity at the receptor THC acts on, and a review of the research notes that it doesn't produce psychoactive effects in people. Heat changes that: smoking, vaping or baking converts THCA into THC, which does. So THCA flower that's smoked behaves like any other cannabis flower.

What happens to THCA when you smoke it?

It turns into THC. The heat of smoking strips a carboxyl group from each THCA molecule, converting it to THC rapidly, and that THC is what you inhale. Not every bit converts or reaches your lungs, so the total THC figure on a label is an upper estimate of what you'll get.

Is THCA flower legal in Michigan?

Only through the licensed system. Michigan law counts THCA as THC, so flower above 0.3% THC, counting THCA, is marijuana that only licensed marijuana businesses may sell, to adults 21 and older or registered patients. Federal hemp rules are also tightening in late 2026. This reflects the law as of October 2026.

Will THCA show up on a drug test?

Plan on it. Smoking, vaping or cooking THCA turns it into THC, which your body breaks down into the compounds cannabis drug tests look for. Even raw THCA products usually contain some THC. If you're subject to testing at work or elsewhere, assume THCA products can lead to a positive result, as any other cannabis can.

How do I calculate total THC from THCA?

Multiply the THCA percentage by 0.877, then add the THC percentage. Flower with 20% THCA and 0.5% THC works out to 0.5 + (20 × 0.877), or about 18% total THC. That 0.877 multiplier reflects the weight THCA loses when heat converts it into THC.
